content.text: The
N+1 problem
never shows up as a slow query. Each statement is cheap; the cost is that the application sends hundreds of them, one
round trip
at a time. From the database side it looks like one tiny statement executed thousands of times, often an exact multiple of another statement's count. Sort Query Store,
sys.dm_exec_query_stats
or
pg_stat_statements
by executions and total time, not by average duration.
The orders page feels sluggish, so someone opens
Query Store

and sorts by average duration. The slowest statement on that page averages 0.18 ms; the others, 0.02 to 0.05 ms. The verdict: "the database is fine, it must be the app." In a test that reproduces the page against SQL Server 2022 in a local Docker container (50 orders, then their lines and their customers), the page took a median of 72 to 75 ms across three runs of 50 page loads. Query Store recorded about 3.5 ms of execution per page. Both numbers are right; the gap between them is the bug.
The common misconception
The belief: if every query a request runs is fast, the database can't be why the request is slow.
It's how database tuning is usually taught: find the slowest query, read its plan, fix it. The tools follow the same idea. PostgreSQL's
log_min_duration_statement

logs only statements that ran at least as long as the threshold, so a 0.05 ms query never appears. A list sorted by average duration puts the heaviest single statement on top. And each of those views is honest; it just answers a different question from "why is this page slow?".
What actually happens
Each statement is a round trip

For every query, the application sends the statement, the server runs it and sends rows back, and the application reads them before it sends the next one. The server measures the middle part, per statement. The time spent travelling between application and database, and the gaps between statements, belong to no query at all, so no per-query statistic can show them.

The test page ran 101 statements: one for the orders, then one for each order's lines and one for each order's customer. Per page, the server executed about 3.5 ms in total; the client waited about 73 ms. The rest, roughly 0.7 ms per statement on this setup, was round trips. That per-trip cost depends on your network and driver, but it's always paid N times, and N grows with the page size.
What the database actually records

The application sent each statement with a parameter, so the database saw one statement text executed many times, not 2,500 different queries. Query Store aggregated it into one entry: 2,500 executions of the lines query, averaging 43 to 48 µs, returning 3 rows each. PostgreSQL's
pg_stat_statements
does the same by design: queries that differ only in their constants are combined into a single entry, with the constants shown as
, and its
calls
column counts the executions.
The fingerprint is in the counts

An N+1 leaves a pattern that's easy to read once you look for it. In the test, the orders query ran 50 times and the lines and customer queries ran 2,500 times each: exactly 50 per execution of the parent, the page size. Each child returned 1 to 3 rows per call. A cheap statement with a high count, few rows per call, and a count that's a clean multiple of another statement's count is a loop in the application, seen from the database.
Averages hide it, and fixing it makes the average look worse
The same page written as one join told the opposite story:

The fix made the page about 40 times faster, and it also made the "slowest query" five to six times slower, because one statement now does the work of 101. A team that judges the database by its slowest average would call the fix a regression.
Look at counts, not averages

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
-- "Which query is slow?" sorted by average duration
SELECT TOP (10) qt.query_sql_text,
       rs.avg_duration / 1000.0 AS avg_ms
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats AS rs
JOIN sys.query_store_plan AS p ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query AS q ON q.query_id = p.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text AS qt
  ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
ORDER BY rs.avg_duration DESC;
-- Tested: the N+1 statements (0.02-0.05 ms) rank last

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
-- How often, how much in total, how many rows each time
SELECT TOP (10) qt.query_sql_text,
       SUM(rs.count_executions) AS executions,
       SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_duration) / 1000 AS total_ms,
       SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_rowcount)
         / SUM(rs.count_executions) AS rows_per_call
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats AS rs
JOIN sys.query_store_plan AS p ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query AS q ON q.query_id = p.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text AS qt
  ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
GROUP BY qt.query_sql_text
ORDER BY executions DESC;
-- Tested: lines query 2,500 runs x 3 rows; orders query 50 runs

content.text: On PostgreSQL,
pg_stat_statements
gives the same view. It needs
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
and
CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements
; the columns below are from the PostgreSQL 18 docs, and the query wasn't run for this article:

blocks.code:
SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 3) AS mean_ms,
       rows / NULLIF(calls, 0) AS rows_per_call, query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY calls DESC
LIMIT 10;

blocks.title: Literal values split the loop into thousands of entries

content.text: If the code builds SQL with the values typed into the text instead of parameters, every order id can become a different statement. In the test, 100 executions of a join with the id written into the text became 100 Query Store queries of 1 execution each. They shared a single
query_hash
, which Microsoft documents for exactly this: aggregating queries that differ only by literal values. Group by
query_hash
, in Query Store or
sys.dm_exec_query_stats
. PostgreSQL merges such constants automatically.

Once you have a suspect, look for its parent: a statement whose execution count divides the suspect's by a small, round number. A ratio equal to your page size, or to the number of items in a typical order, tells you which endpoint has the loop before you open the code.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Sort by executions and total time

content.text: Make the weekly check in Query Store or
pg_stat_statements
sort by execution count and total duration. Look for statements with tiny averages near the top.
For each suspect, find the statement whose count divides it cleanly, and check the rows per call. That pair is the loop and its parent.

Replace the loop with a join or a projection, or batch the ids into one query. For EF Core, the .NET path's article "Beyond Include: Fixing N+1 in EF Core With Projections and Split Queries" covers the code side.
After the fix, the statement count per request should drop and the client-side latency should follow, even if the slowest average goes up.
Key takeaways

items.text: A fast query can still make a slow page: the cost of N+1 is round trips, which no per-query statistic includes.
In the test, the page waited about 73 ms while the server executed about 3.5 ms of it.
The database records an N+1 as one parameterized statement with a huge count and few rows per call, often an exact multiple of another statement's count.
Sort by executions and total time; sorting by average duration ranks N+1 last and makes the fix look like a regression.
